strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem: LLM-based text augmentation can silently delete or fabricate clinically critical content, and prior causal-augmentation work (e.g., CATO) does not guard against this.

The proposed pipeline (lightweight NER-based 'weak expert' supplies a preserve-list to the rewriting LLM) is simple, computationally cheap, requires no additional training, and is clearly described with prompts provided in the appendix.

Evaluation spans multiple axes: entity preservation/hallucination rates, three supervised MIMIC-III prediction tasks with two downstream architectures, zero/one/few-shot phenotyping and ICD retrieval, ablations over weak-expert and generalist models, and a DPO-based single-model distillation variant.

The honest reporting that the DPO-distilled 'Strong Expert' does not consistently close the gap with the dual-model pipeline (Table 5), and the discussion of when weak-expert calibration matters (Section 6), add credibility.

The core finding — that even an imperfect general NER model as supervisor improves augmentation quality (Table 4) — is an interesting and potentially useful observation connected to weak-supervision literature.
weaknesses: Circular evaluation of the central safety claim: PR and HR are computed with the same entity extractor (biomedical-ner-all) that generates the preservation constraints Ki. Since the method explicitly instructs the LLM to keep these entities verbatim, high PR/low HR are largely baked in by construction, and baseline methods are disadvantaged. The safety evidence does not independently support the 'reduced factual errors' claim.

The PR/HR metrics themselves are questionable proxies for 'safety': legitimate synonym substitution (e.g., fever→pyrexia) would count as hallucination, and clinically false statements that are not named entities (e.g., flipped negations, altered temporal qualifiers) are invisible to the metric. No human or clinician evaluation of augmented notes is performed.

Statistical support for downstream gains is weak: standard errors are large and overlapping (e.g., readmission 0.599±0.03 vs. CATO 0.552±0.04 with Qwen-3), no significance tests are reported, Table 1 uses only 300 samples, and some reported numbers are hard to interpret (e.g., Zero-Shot length-of-stay RMSE of 73.277 vs. ~15–18 for trained models).

Baselines are narrow: only a naive paraphrase prompt and CATO. Missing comparisons include simple constrained/verified decoding, post-hoc filtering of naive augmentations with the same NER tool (which would directly test whether the 'collaboration' adds anything over rejection sampling), and other LLM augmentation methods cited in the related work.

The causal framing (Figure 3, V vs. U) is decorative: no causal graph is specified or used, V is operationalized simply as NER-extracted medical entities, and the gap between the 'causally driven' theory and the keyword-preservation implementation is not bridged.

The novelty is limited: the method amounts to prompt engineering with NER-extracted keyword lists plus standard DPO distillation; framing this as a 'novel model collaboration framework' injecting 'expert-level domain knowledge' overstates what a span-level entity tagger provides (it cannot verify clinical validity, only surface presence).

Presentation is below bar for a main-track submission: leftover editing notes appear in the appendix ('Training details – add details on SFT and DPO'), numerous typos ('et modifies', 't avoids', 'rresults', 'LlaMA'), inconsistent citation of CATO as Feder et al. 2022 vs. 2023, a duplicated Zhou et al. reference (2023/2024), and inconsistencies between the stated default generalist (Qwen-3-0.6B) and the models actually used in the safety table (Llama-3.2-1B/3B).

Ethics and limitations treatment is thin: no discussion in the main text of risks of deploying synthetic clinical data, no mention of MIMIC-III data-use/credentialing constraints or privacy considerations, and limitations are relegated to an appendix 'Future Work' section.
Reproducibility claims (seeds, scripts, hyperparameter grids 'released') are made without links or artifacts, and MIMIC-III's access restrictions further complicate independent verification.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: safety-aware LLM-based data augmentation for clinical text, where hallucination and loss of critical information have real consequences.
The core idea is simple and sensible: use a lightweight domain NER model to identify safety-critical tokens and inject them as explicit preservation constraints into the rewriting prompt.

Evaluation spans a reasonably broad set of clinical tasks (readmission, mortality, length-of-stay, phenotyping, ICD coding) and multiple downstream architectures (Qwen-3, BERT) and generalist models (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen, GPT-4o, Claude).

The component analysis (Table 4) on weak-expert specialization and the DPO-based distillation experiment (Table 5) add some empirical depth, and the paper honestly reports that the single-model Strong Expert does not consistently match the dual-model pipeline.
Limitations and failure modes are discussed (calibration of the weak expert, backbone dependence of RL distillation).
weaknesses: Serious circularity in the central safety evaluation: the same entity-extraction tool E(.) is used both to construct the preservation constraints Ki and to compute the Preservation Rate and Hallucination Rate (Appendix A.3 explicitly states this). The method thus optimizes its own evaluation metric by construction, so Table 1 cannot be taken as independent evidence of 'safer' augmentation.

Confounded comparison from filtering: Appendix A.3 states candidates are accepted 'only when PR meets or exceeds tau_PR and HR is at or below tau_HR'. If this filtering applies to the proposed method (it is not stated for baselines), the headline quality gains in Table 1 are partly a post-hoc selection effect rather than a property of the query-based guidance. A natural, missing baseline is naive augmentation filtered by the same NER tool.

The causal framing (Figure 3, V vs U, 'prior causal graph') is largely decorative: in practice V is simply the set of NER-extracted biomedical entities, and no expert-specified causal graph or task-specific identification of critical variables is ever used. The formalization in Section 4 does not add technical content beyond 'append the keyword list to the prompt'.

Weak baselines: comparisons are limited to naive paraphrasing and CATO. Stronger and more relevant alternatives (e.g., constrained decoding, self-consistency checks, post-hoc rejection sampling with an NER verifier, or other domain-guided augmentation methods) are absent, making it hard to attribute gains to the collaboration framework specifically.

Statistical and consistency concerns: improvements on some tasks are within reported standard errors (e.g., Qwen-3 mortality 0.917+/-0.02 vs. 0.910+/-0.03); no significance tests are reported; Table 4's CATO HR (0.77) is inconsistent with Table 1's settings; Table 5 relabels length-of-stay as 'Period (RMSE)'; the appendix grid search says 3 epochs is best (Acc. 0.615) yet the main-table result is the 1-epoch value (0.599), an unexplained discrepancy. Quality metrics are computed on only 300 samples.

Presentation is rough for a main-track submission: leftover editing artifacts ('Training details – add details on SFT and DPO'), multiple typos ('et modifies', 't avoids', 'rresults', 'LlaMA'), and inconsistent terminology throughout.

The DPO extension is under-specified (preference-pair construction details, hyperparameters, and training compute are not given), and since the safety metrics are circular, the Strong Expert results inherit the same evaluation problems.

Reproducibility claims are made (fixed seeds, released scripts), but no code or artifact link is provided in the manuscript, and several key details (filtering thresholds tau_PR/tau_HR, number of augmented samples used for training) are missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: preserving domain-critical information during LLM-based text augmentation in safety-critical (clinical) settings, with a clear motivation grounded in causal augmentation (Feder et al., 2023).

The proposed pipeline is simple, lightweight, and training-free (a clinical NER model supplies token-preservation constraints to an instruction-tuned rewriter), which makes it practical and easy to adopt.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: three MIMIC-III prediction tasks (readmission, mortality, length-of-stay), zero/one/few-shot phenotyping and ICD coding, multiple generalist models (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen-3), two downstream architectures (Qwen-3 with LoRA, BERT), and an ablation over weak-expert designs (Table 4).

The extension distilling the dual-model collaboration into a single DPO-trained 'Strong Expert' (Table 5) is an interesting idea, and the paper honestly reports that the distilled model does not consistently match the dual-model pipeline.
The limitations and future work discussion (Section A.4) is candid, and the appendix provides prompts, hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 6-8), and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the framing: the core mechanism is a prompt template that lists entities extracted by an NER model and asks the LLM to preserve them. Framing this as a 'query-based model collaboration framework' with 'weak expert' and 'strong generalist' overstates a fairly standard constrained-prompting recipe. No comparison to obvious alternatives such as constrained decoding, post-hoc filtering/rejection, or simply prompting a stronger LLM to 'preserve all medical entities' without an external NER model.

The central safety evaluation is circular: Preservation Rate and Hallucination Rate (Eq. 3) are computed with the same NER tool used to generate the constraints K_i. A method that enforces verbatim copying of the extractor's outputs will trivially score well on PR, and the reported PR/HR gaps may largely reflect this. An independent evaluation (human expert review, a different entity extractor, or factuality metrics) is needed to substantiate the safety claims.

Weak baselines: only 'Naive' paraphrasing and CATO are compared. There are no comparisons to other hallucination-mitigation or constrained-generation approaches, nor to few-shot constrained prompting variants that could match the method's performance without any auxiliary model, which is essential to establish that the 'expert model' component is the causal driver rather than simply adding 'preserve medical terms' instructions.

Several headline results are not statistically convincing: downstream gains are small relative to reported standard errors (e.g., mortality with Qwen-3: 0.917±0.02 vs. 0.910±0.03; with BERT, CATO achieves 0.923±0.003 vs. Ours 0.929±0.03, an overlap well within error), and no significance tests are reported. The readmission gain (+0.047 over CATO) is the strongest result, but it appears only in one of six model-task combinations.

Reported details and internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Table 5 labels the length-of-stay column 'Period (RMSE)' inconsistently with Table 2; Table 4 shows CATO with higher HR (0.77) than Naive (0.59) without explanation; the acceptance thresholds tau_PR/tau_HR in Appendix A.3 are never given values; dataset sizes, number of augmented samples per original, and compute costs of augmentation are not reported.

The zero/one/few-shot evaluation protocol is conceptually unclear: it is not explained how augmented training data relates to 'zero-shot inference' on phenotyping (Figure 5), and ICD coding F1 scores (~0.19) are low, making small differences hard to interpret clinically or practically.

Presentation issues: typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., 'et modifies its non-critical tokens', 't avoids distorting', 'rresults'), and Figure 2's qualitative example is illustrative rather than evidence; only a single cherry-picked synthetic example is shown without quantitative qualitative-analysis sampling.

The 'causal' framing (Section 3, Figure 3) is largely decorative: the method never uses a causal graph or any causal analysis; V is operationalized as generic biomedical NER entities, so the connection to counterfactual/causal augmentation is asserted rather than realized.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and important problem: LLM-based data augmentation in safety-critical domains where hallucinated or deleted medical information is harmful. The framing around preserving critical (V) vs. perturbable (U) variables is clear and well-motivated.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this kind of method paper: multiple downstream tasks (readmission, mortality, length-of-stay), zero/one/few-shot transfer to phenotyping and ICD coding, ablations over both weak-expert and strong-generalist components (Tables 3-5), robustness checks with alternative PR/HR estimators (Table 5), a cost/compute analysis (Table 12, Appendix A.5), and a DPO-based distillation extension (Table 6).
Human validation with three clinical experts (Fleiss' Kappa reported, Table 11) corroborates the automated PR/HR metrics, addressing the concern that NER-based evaluation may be evaluator-specific.

Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge the weak expert's recall limits, the circularity risk of the estimator, the modest and inconsistent distillation gains, and show failure cases (Figure 6) where implicit critical content is missed.
Reproducibility statement is concrete: prompts, acceptance thresholds, hyperparameter grids, seeds, and scripts are described in detail (Appendix A.1-A.3).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: at its core, the method extracts keywords with an off-the-shelf clinical NER model and instructs an instruction-tuned LLM to preserve them verbatim. This is essentially constrained prompting; the 'weak expert guiding strong generalist' framing (borrowed from weak-to-strong generalization) somewhat overstates the conceptual machinery relative to what is actually done.

The theoretical guarantee in Section 4 is nearly vacuous: the bound r*eps + (1-r)*p_c < p_c is elementary probability algebra restating that conditional preservation reduces corruption. It provides little insight beyond intuition.

Strict verbatim preservation of all extracted entities raises a real concern about augmentation diversity: the augmented samples are largely stylistic rewrites, so it is unclear whether downstream gains stem from genuine augmentation (variance reduction, counterfactual coverage) rather than a form of data duplication. The paper does not measure diversity of the augmented corpus.

Downstream improvements are modest and sometimes within or near one standard error (e.g., mortality 0.917+-0.002 vs. 0.912+-0.002 for Qwen-3; several BERT comparisons), and the baselines are limited to paraphrase-style augmentation; stronger data-selection or verification-based augmentation baselines are absent.

Evaluation is confined to MIMIC-III; claims about generalization across institutions and domains (Discussion) are not supported by cross-dataset experiments, and the method's applicability beyond clinical NER (law, finance) is only asserted.
Human evaluation covers only 26 annotated discharge summaries, which is a small sample for gold-standard safety validation.

Presentation has notable sloppiness: several typos ('save our method', 'otdomain-critical', garbled text in Figure 1 examples), an AWS EC2 pricing citation, and a boilerplate impact statement that does not engage with the specific ethical issues of synthetic clinical text generation despite the paper's own safety framing.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: safe LLM-based data augmentation for high-stakes clinical text, and the framing around preserving critical domain variables V while perturbing non-critical variables U is a reasonable problem formulation.

Empirical evaluation is broad: augmentation quality (PR/HR at token and concept levels), three downstream prediction tasks, zero/one/few-shot phenotyping and ICD retrieval, ablations over weak-expert and generalist choices, and robustness checks with alternative NER estimators (Table 5).

The paper includes human expert annotation (three trained nurses, Fleiss' Kappa reported in A.4), a qualitative comparison (Figure 6, including an honest failure case), and an inference-time-only cost analysis (Table 12), which is more thorough than many augmentation papers.

The limitations are discussed candidly in several places, e.g., the inconsistent DPO distillation results across backbones in Section 5.5 and the open challenge of detecting implicit critical content in A.4.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method essentially reduces to running an off-the-shelf biomedical NER model, inserting its extracted entities into the prompt as 'preserve these keywords', and having an LLM rephrase. The 'query-based model collaboration' framing substantially oversells what is constrained prompting; no model is trained until the supplementary DPO experiment, which itself is acknowledged as inconsistent and an open question.

Circularity between method and evaluation: the primary PR/HR results (Tables 2, 3, 4, 12) use biomedical-ner-all both as the weak expert that defines the constraint set and as the quality estimator. Although Table 5 mitigates this by showing trends under alternative estimators, the headline numbers likely flatter the method, and the candidate filtering step (discarding samples below a preservation threshold in A.3) introduces further potential evaluation bias not applied to baselines.

The theoretical bound (expected corruption rε + (1−r)pc < pc when ε < pc) is trivial algebra presented as a theoretical justification; its assumptions (independence, fixed violation probability) are neither analyzed nor empirically estimated.

Downstream gains are modest and statistical significance is not established: e.g., mortality accuracy 0.929±0.03 (Ours) vs 0.923±0.003 (CATO) has overlapping error bars; accuracy-only reporting for readmission/mortality is unusual given class imbalance (AUROC/AUPRC are standard); large standard errors (e.g., length-of-stay ±5.29) suggest the results may be underpowered.
The human validation is thin: 26 discharge summary notes annotated by trained nurses (not physicians), with moderate agreement for readmission (κ=0.437).

There are red flags in the references, e.g., Cho et al. 2026 with 'arXiv:2605.28129', an impossible arXiv identifier, plus typos ('t avoids', 'ofdomain-critical') that suggest insufficient proofreading and raise concerns about citation hygiene.

The cost analysis (A.5) partly argues against a strawman: the relevant competing baselines here (naive prompting, CATO) are also inference-time methods, and the claimed savings versus SFT are not central to the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: hallucination and information distortion in LLM-based augmentation for safety-critical domains, with a concrete clinical instantiation (MIMIC-III notes).

The proposed framework is simple, lightweight, and deployable: a NER-based 'weak expert' extracts critical tokens that are injected as verbatim preservation constraints into the generalist LLM's prompt. The design is easy to reproduce and the cost analysis (Table 12) credibly shows the overhead (~18% over naive augmentation) is modest.

Evaluation is multi-pronged: automated entity/concept-level PR and HR metrics with multiple NER estimators (Tables 2-5), downstream tasks across two architectures (Table 1), zero/few-shot phenotyping and ICD retrieval (Figure 3, Table 10), human clinician annotation with Fleiss' Kappa (Table 11), component ablations over weak experts and generalists, and a cost analysis.

The paper is generally well organized, with a clear problem formulation distinguishing critical (V) vs. non-critical (U) variables, honest qualitative failure analysis (Figure 6), and an explicit discussion of limitations and future work (A.6).
The distillation extension via DPO (Table 6) is an interesting attempt to test whether the collaboration signal can be internalized, and the negative/mixed results are reported candidly.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method reduces to prompting the LLM with a list of NER-extracted entities to preserve verbatim. Framing this as a 'query-based model collaboration framework' with 'expert-level domain knowledge' overstates a straightforward constrained-prompting pipeline. The causal-graph framing (Figure 5) is conceptual only and never operationalized in the method or experiments.

The theoretical contribution is thin. The corruption bound r*eps + (1-r)*p_c < p_c is an immediate consequence of the setup, makes assumptions never validated empirically (e.g., preservation violations being independent), and the paper provides no measurement of r or eps on real data.

Evidence of downstream gains is weaker than claimed. In Table 1, several improvements are small relative to reported standard errors (e.g., Qwen-3 mortality 0.917±0.02 vs. Biomedical LLM 0.912±0.02), and no statistical significance testing is reported. Figure 3 lacks error bars. The consistent-but-modest gains would benefit from significance analysis.

Potential circularity in the safety evaluation. The biomedical-ner-all model both generates the constraints K_i and serves as the PR/HR estimator in Tables 3, 4, and 12, which could bias quality metrics toward the method. The alternative-estimator ablation (Table 5) mitigates but does not eliminate this concern, and human validation covers only 26 notes.

A citation integrity red flag: the reference 'Cho, D., Zhang, M., and Chunara, R. Do clinical models change treatment decisions?, 2026. arXiv:2605.28129' cites an arXiv ID (2605) that postdates the submission window and appears not to exist; this pattern is consistent with an unverified/LLM-hallucinated reference. There are also miscitations (e.g., 'Jiang et al., 2023' given as the source of BERT when it is NYUTron; BERT has no Devlin citation), which raise concerns about reference diligence.

The augmentation preserves all medical entities verbatim, which by the paper's own formulation means only style/phrasing (U) is varied. This makes the framing as counterfactual/structure-aware augmentation somewhat inconsistent, and raises the question of how much genuine diversity the augmented data adds beyond paraphrase.
Single-dataset evaluation (MIMIC-III only) limits support for the broader claim of applicability to 'specialized domains' (law, finance), which remains future work.

Reproducibility is asserted ('we release the hyperparameter grids and scripts') but no repository or artifact link is provided in the manuscript; MIMIC-III's credentialing further limits independent replication.

Writing has multiple typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 't avoids', 'set ofdomain-critical', mixed patient names 'Doe'/'John' in the synthetic Figure 1 example, inconsistent baseline citation numbers [1]/[20]/[21]/[35] with no numbered bibliography), suggesting the manuscript needs another careful pass.
